newsitem.title: USA: Sentencing phase to start in Oklahoma bomb trial.
newsitem.headline: Sentencing phase to start in Oklahoma bomb trial.

text.p: Jurors begin considering on Wednesday whether Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh will be executed or will spend his life in prison, and is expected to hear some of the most heart-wrenching testimony so far.
A 10-year-old boy is among those scheduled to testify. He plans to tell the jury about losing his mother in the April 19, 1995 bombing, prosecutors said.
The trial's penalty phase comes in the wake of Monday's verdict that found McVeigh guilty of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people and wounding more than 500 others.
The same jurors now must decide whether McVeigh lives or dies, and attorneys for both sides argued before Judge Richard Matsch on Tuesday about what evidence and testimony they would hear.

A volunteer rescue worker plans to tell about the last minutes of life of a woman dying in the rubble of the collapsed building, prosecutors said. Holding her hand, "he literally felt her pulse stop and she died," said prosecutor Sean Connelly. Another rescuer will describe his recurring nightmares.
The prosecution said it plans to call as many as 45 witnesses, probably over three days. Most will create brief snapshots of lost loved ones, taking 10 to 15 minutes apiece.
Others will be people scarred for a lifetime by the explosion, which the government said McVeigh, an embittered former soldier, caused out of hatred for the U.S. government.
The jurors will see family portraits and a photograph of toddlers playing in the building's daycare centre. In that poignant picture are faces of children who died in the blast.

They will hear the stories of more than two dozen people who suffered near-fatal injuries, see a man whose face was forever disfigured and watch a videotape made outside a hospital emergency room, the dead and dying on stretchers and gurneys.

Oklahoma's medical examiner will run through an assortment of ways that the bombing victims died, such as crushing, dismemberment and suffocation. He will describe those who did not die so quickly, including a man who perished from gravel imbedded in his lungs.

On Tuesday, with the jury off for the day, Judge Richard Matsch ruled out descriptions by family members of identifying bodies; he banned funeral photos, diaries, a poem by a victim's father and a video made at the Murrah building's credit union. The video showed seven people who would soon die.
He vetoed talk of a service in which a victim's family placed a rose at the bomb site and set free a lone white dove.
"I don't believe that's the type of thing the jury should consider," Matsch said.
Deciding what is introduced in the sentencing phase is a fragile process, he said, with a fine line between "appropriate testimony" and that motivated by "passion, revenge and rage."
The jury must produce "a truly moral response to appropriate information as opposed to an emotional response," he said.

Prosecutors sought to introduce as much evidence as they could as so-called aggravating factors that would tilt the jury toward the death penalty. Such factors can include premeditated murder and the deaths of law enforcement agents.
The defence countered by trying to limit the extent of that testimony against their client.
Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones has not revealed whether he will put McVeigh on the stand, and many legal experts feel that scenario is an unlikely one.

Observers say the defence is likely to call his father or sister to recount McVeigh's upbringing and introduce his record as a U.S. Army sergeant during the Gulf War. McVeigh betrayed little emotion during his trial and the reading of the verdict.

"Jones's great challenge is to show the jury he's not just a monster but a human being as well," said legal expert Robert Precht, who has followed the trial. "He must convey to the jury this person's humanity. It's going to be a tall order."
